solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Many labels changed using every available method

indicators.note: something changed has been altered, so the letters are put into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, ten letters

explanation.surface: Someone relabels lots of stock in every way they can think of.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of 'Many labels' rearrange exactly into the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for doing something in whatever way possible, with any method at hand.

clue.text: Proclamation involving shout that startles thicko

indicators.note: to involve is to include or take in, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a ban is an official proclamation forbidding something
the shout you make to give someone a fright

explanation.surface: An announcement includes a shout that frightens a dim person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thicko' is British slang for a stupid person; the startling shout is the one used to make someone jump.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a great ape is a common insult meaning a clumsy, stupid oaf.

clue.text: Highest point in a river – Ganges’s source?

blocks.note: taken as written
the Po is the great river of northern Italy
the source of 'Ganges' is its first letter, G, spelt out as a word

explanation.surface: A question about where a river reaches its peak, and where the Ganges starts.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the trick: the start of Ganges is the letter G, and a letter written as a word is GEE.
explanation.definitionFit: An apogee is the farthest point of an orbit, and by extension the peak or climax of anything.

clue.text: Seductive story also penned by Welsh Dante, a drunk

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about out of order, so these letters lurch into a new arrangement
something penned is shut in a pen, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: taken as written, eleven letters to rearrange
'and' means also, in addition

explanation.surface: A tipsy Welsh Dante writes a tale of seduction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Welsh Dante, a' rearranges to LEDA THE SWAN, and AND slips into the gap. 'Drunk' here is a noun, but still signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Zeus took the form of a swan to seduce Leda; Yeats's sonnet of this title retells it.

clue.text: Change examination to accommodate current leader

indicators.note: to accommodate a guest is to give them room, so one piece takes another inside

blocks.note: to edit is to change a text
an oral is a spoken exam
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: An exam is altered to make room for the present leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current leader' reads as today's boss; current is really I, and 'leader' alone is the definition. EDIT then OR(I)AL.
explanation.definitionFit: In British newspapers a leader, or leading article, is the editorial column giving the paper's own opinion.

clue.text: Canoodles and kisses where knight supplants page

indicators.note: to supplant is to oust and take the place of, so one letter is swapped for another

blocks.note: N is the chess notation for a knight
pecks are quick kisses; its P (page) is the letter replaced

explanation.surface: Romance in a medieval court: a knight takes the page's place for kisses.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the abbreviation for page; swap it for N, the chess symbol for knight, and PECKS turns into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To neck is informal British slang for kissing and cuddling, the same as to canoodle.

clue.text: Exploited European employed in Bucks?

indicators.note: someone employed in a firm works inside it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: US dollars, colloquially bucks, abbreviated as the currency code
E is the standard abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A European worker in Buckinghamshire is taken advantage of.
explanation.walkthrough: Bucks looks like Buckinghamshire, an English county; the question mark says it is dollars, USD. E goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To exploit someone is to make selfish use of them, so exploited and used share this sense.

clue.text: Sloppy start to Scarborough Fair around noon

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
to go around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: first letter
fair in the old sense of beautiful
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: The Scarborough Fair, from the folk song, got off to a messy start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scarborough Fair' reads as the song title; split it: S, then fair as LOVELY, wrapped around N.
explanation.definitionFit: Slovenly describes someone careless and untidy in habits or appearance, much like sloppy.

clue.text: 500 explorers vacated ancient city’s ruins

indicators.note: a vacated room has been emptied, so the insides go and only the outside letters stay

blocks.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500
first and last letters
Troy is the ancient city of the Iliad; the 's adds S

explanation.surface: Hundreds of explorers have left the ruins of an old city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruins' looks like a noun about the city's remains; it is the verb that defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ruin something is to wreck it completely, so ruins and destroys are verb synonyms.

clue.text: Unhinged Lear’s twentieth Stratford production?

indicators.note: something unhinged is deranged and off its fixings, so the letters fall into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, fourteen letters

explanation.surface: A mad King Lear as the twentieth play staged at Stratford.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear is a Shakespeare play, which pulls you towards play titles, but the name is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: This late Shakespeare romance is regularly staged by the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon, the playwright's birthplace.

clue.text: Such a route, as a rule, is not wide

definitions.text: Such a route, as a rule, is not wide

blocks.clueFragment: Such a route, as a rule, is not wide
blocks.note: surface reading: a remark about some narrow kind of road
setter's reading: split the word into a letter plus 'road', the British class of minor road, usually narrow

explanation.surface: An observation that a certain type of road is generally narrow.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain A roads are main roads and B roads are minor country ones. Read as B ROAD, the word meaning 'wide' names a road that usually is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Split in two, the letters name a class of British minor road, typically narrow and winding.

clue.text: Old Peruvian comedians collaborating

blocks.note: the Inca empire ruled Peru before the Spanish conquest
a hoot is a very funny person

explanation.surface: Some ancient Peruvian comics working together on an act.
explanation.walkthrough: A hoot, informally, is someone hilarious, so comedians are HOOTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in cahoots means working secretly together with someone, usually on something dubious.

clue.text: Herb‘s old ass going backwards

indicators.note: going backwards means travelling the wrong way, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
the onager is a wild ass of Asia

explanation.surface: Someone called Herb owns an elderly donkey that keeps reversing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herb' looks like a man's name; it is the definition. The ass is the onager, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregano is an aromatic Mediterranean plant whose leaves are used to flavour cooking, a classic kitchen herb.

clue.text: Silk purse not from this, so Don invests shillings

indicators.note: to invest someone is to clothe them, so one piece is wrapped round another

blocks.note: taken as written
to don clothes is to put them on and wear them
S is the abbreviation for shillings, the old British coin

explanation.surface: A university don puts shillings into a project that cannot be turned into luxury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don invests shillings' sounds like an academic putting money in; Don is the verb WEAR, which clothes S.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says you can't make a silk purse out of a sow's ear: fine things cannot come from poor material.

clue.text: “Daddy” heartless in Lolita, criminal as well

indicators.note: something without a heart has lost its centre, so the middle letter goes
criminal behaviour is crooked and wrong, so the letters go out of their proper order

blocks.note: the word with its central letter dropped
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dark remark about the father figure in Nabokov's novel being a criminal too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a placement word, but its two letters join the mix with DADY and LOLITA.
explanation.definitionFit: Additionally and as well both mean also or in addition, adding a further point.

clue.text: Hospital admitted woman wrapped around tree

indicators.note: a wrapping goes around its contents, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a patient admitted is let in
a common woman's name
a common conifer

explanation.surface: A hospital takes in a woman who has crashed into a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hospital admitted' reads as one phrase, but 'Hospital' is the definition and 'admitted' starts the wordplay, joined to the woman as one wrapper.
explanation.definitionFit: An infirmary is a place caring for the sick, an older word still used in many British hospital names.

clue.text: Broomstick riders after small and flexible twigs

indicators.note: coming after something places it second, which fixes the order of the parts

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
witches are pictured flying on broomsticks

explanation.surface: Witches' brooms are made from small bendy twigs.
explanation.walkthrough: The broomstick picture suits the twigs a broom is made of, which hides that the definition is at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A switch is a thin, pliable stick or shoot cut from a tree, once used for whipping.

clue.text: Work ending so claimed Universal Credit?

indicators.note: to work material is to knead and reshape it, so the letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, eight letters

explanation.surface: Someone loses their job and so applies for state benefits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work' looks like a noun for a job but is the verb signalling the rearrangement. Universal Credit is the UK welfare benefit, claimed after work ends.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain registering at the jobcentre to claim unemployment benefit is described by this phrasal verb.

clue.text: One trying to raise the bar with crew and Jack?

definitions.text: One trying to raise the bar

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for with
a rowing eight is a boat crew
simply joins the parts
a jack is a device for lifting a car

explanation.surface: Someone aiming to improve standards with their team and Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise the bar' is the idiom for improving standards; read literally it is lifting a barbell.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitor in this sport literally hoists a loaded barbell above their head.

clue.text: Legendary king in craft wounded – time to go

indicators.note: telling something it is time to go means it must leave, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: art means skill or craft
hurt, minus its T for time

explanation.surface: A mythical king lies injured in a boat as the time comes to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: T is the abbreviation for time; dropping it from HURT leaves HUR after ART.
explanation.definitionFit: King Arthur of Camelot and the Round Table is the legendary British ruler of medieval romance.

clue.text: News during Christmas about famed Liverpudlian

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the letters run backwards
what happens during a period falls within it, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: N is short for new, so two of them make news
Noel is another word for Christmas

explanation.surface: A news story at Christmas about a celebrity from Liverpool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' sits between the parts as if it meant 'concerning'; really it turns the Christmas word round. Two Ns make 'news' as new plus new.
explanation.definitionFit: John Lennon of the Beatles was born and raised in Liverpool, so he is a celebrated native of that city.

clue.text: Land fish that’s caught in ship regularly

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every other one, so alternate letters are kept
something caught is held inside, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: a large sea fish
first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: Bring ashore a fish that keeps getting caught on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a placement word, but it is part of the source: alternate letters of 'in ship' give ISI, held in TUNA.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunisia is a North African country, and land is a common crossword word for a nation.

clue.text: Trouble as wrecked Argo ships gallons

indicators.note: to ship cargo is to carry it aboard, so one piece is taken inside another
a wrecked thing is smashed apart, so its letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
G is the abbreviation for gallons

explanation.surface: Jason's ship the Argo founders while carrying a heavy cargo of fluid.
explanation.walkthrough: Argo is the ship of Jason and the Argonauts; it takes in G and the five letters are then rearranged. Aggro is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggro is informal British slang for aggressive behaviour, hassle or fighting, so trouble fits.

clue.text: Minister once again to hold back

blocks.note: the prefix meaning again
to minister to is to serve

explanation.surface: A former cabinet minister is back in government, then told to restrain themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' looks like a noun, a politician, but here it is the verb meaning to attend to someone's needs.
explanation.definitionFit: To reserve something is to keep it aside for later rather than use it now.

clue.text: Bush ranger skinned that monster devours

indicators.note: skinning removes the outer layer, so the first and last letters are stripped
to devour is to swallow whole, so one piece ends up inside another

blocks.note: the many-headed serpent of Greek myth
the word minus its outer letters

explanation.surface: An Australian bush ranger is flayed and eaten by a beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush ranger' reads as an outback outlaw; split it: 'Bush' is the definition and 'ranger' loses its skin.
explanation.definitionFit: The hydrangea is a flowering garden shrub with large rounded heads of blooms.

clue.text: Arsenic added to chicken pasty

blocks.note: As is the chemical symbol for arsenic
a hen is a female chicken

explanation.surface: Poison slipped into a chicken pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken pasty' reads as a pie; pasty is really the adjective meaning pale.
explanation.definitionFit: A pasty face is pale and unhealthy-looking, the same as an ashen complexion drained of colour.

clue.text: Degenerate son with tattoos

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
to ink someone is to tattoo them

explanation.surface: A wayward son covered in tattoos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Degenerate' reads as an adjective or noun for the son; it is the verb, and 'tattoos' is a verb too.
explanation.definitionFit: To sink morally is to decline or deteriorate, which is what degenerate means as a verb.

clue.text: Solid figure picked up parrot and wader around delta

indicators.note: a sound picked up is heard rather than seen, so the word counts by its sound
going around something encircles it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: Polly is the stock name for a pet parrot
a long-legged wading bird
Delta is D in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Somebody lifts a parrot and a wading bird by the river mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Polly is the name traditionally given to parrots; said aloud it gives the Greek prefix for many. HERON wraps round D.
explanation.definitionFit: A polyhedron is a three-dimensional shape bounded by many flat faces, such as a cube or pyramid.
